claim: Salamanders are unparalleled among tetrapods in their ability to regenerate many structures, including entire limbs.
source: Salamanders are unparalleled among tetrapods in their ability to regenerate many structures, including entire limbs, and the study of this ability may provide insights into human regenerative therapies.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about salamander regenerative capabilities.

claim: The study of salamander limb regeneration may provide insights into human regenerative therapies.
source: Salamanders are unparalleled among tetrapods in their ability to regenerate many structures, including entire limbs, and the study of this ability may provide insights into human regenerative therapies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the research.

claim: Using CRISPR/Cas, unique cell lineages within the developing axolotl embryo can be genetically labelled.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas, we genetically labelled unique cell lineages within the developing axolotl embryo and tracked the frequency of each lineage within amputated and fully regenerated limbs.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The frequency of each lineage within amputated and fully regenerated limbs can be tracked.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas, we genetically labelled unique cell lineages within the developing axolotl embryo and tracked the frequency of each lineage within amputated and fully regenerated limbs.
evidence: This describes the experimental method and results of the study.

claim: This approach allows assessment of the contributions of multiple low frequency cell lineages to the regenerating limb at once for the first time.
source: This allowed us, for the first time, to assess the contributions of multiple low frequency cell lineages to the regenerating limb at once.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Regenerated limbs are high fidelity replicas of the originals even after repeated amputations.
source: Our comparisons reveal that regenerated limbs are high fidelity replicas of the originals even after repeated amputations.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The origin of the cells of the blastema has long been the subject of debate.
source: The origin of the cells of the blastema, the mass of proliferating cells that gives rise to regenerated structures, has long been the subject of debate (Tanaka and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The blastema is the mass of proliferating cells that gives rise to regenerated structures.
source: The origin of the cells of the blastema, the mass of proliferating cells that gives rise to regenerated structures, has long been the subject of debate (Tanaka and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In salamanders, the debate about blastema origin has centered on whether the limb blastema arises from dedifferentiated cells or proliferating stem cells.
source: In salamanders, such as the axolotl, this debate has centered on whether the limb blastema arises from dedifferentiated cells or proliferating stem cells (Tanaka, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Earlier studies using tissue grafts suggested that restricted tissue types, such as dermis or cartilage, can give rise to some or all of the other tissues in regenerated limbs.
source: Earlier studies using tissue grafts suggested that restricted tissue types, such as dermis or cartilage, can give rise to some or all of the other tissues in regenerated limbs (Namenwirth, 1974; Muneoka et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More recent work using GFP-labelled grafts found little evidence of lineage switching during limb regeneration, though dermis may contribute to cartilage and tendons.
source: More recent work using GFP-labelled grafts found little evidence of lineage switching during limb regeneration, though dermis may contribute to cartilage and tendons (Kragl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A study using tissue grafting and in vivo imaging of single cells during digit tip regeneration suggests that dedifferentiated or proliferative chondrocytes contribute very little to regeneration.
source: A study using tissue grafting and in vivo imaging of single cells during digit tip regeneration further suggests that dedifferentiated or proliferative chondrocytes contribute very little to regeneration, and these cells are most likely replenished by dermal fibroblasts (Currie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Chondrocytes are most likely replenished by dermal fibroblasts during digit tip regeneration.
source: A study using tissue grafting and in vivo imaging of single cells during digit tip regeneration further suggests that dedifferentiated or proliferative chondrocytes contribute very little to regeneration, and these cells are most likely replenished by dermal fibroblasts (Currie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Axolotls and larval newts regenerate muscle by recruiting satellite cells to the blastema.
source: Comparisons of muscle regeneration between species of salamanders have shown that axolotls and larval newts regenerate muscle by recruiting satellite cells to the blastema; however, fragmentation and cell cycle reentry of myofibers provides the cellular source of regenerated muscle in adult newts (Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fragmentation and cell cycle reentry of myofibers provides the cellular source of regenerated muscle in adult newts.
source: Comparisons of muscle regeneration between species of salamanders have shown that axolotls and larval newts regenerate muscle by recruiting satellite cells to the blastema; however, fragmentation and cell cycle reentry of myofibers provides the cellular source of regenerated muscle in adult newts (Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Salamander limb regeneration is governed by numerous tissue- and life-cycle-dependent mechanisms.
source: This long history of grafting studies of salamander limb regeneration demonstrates that this process is governed by numerous tissue- and life-cycle-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on grafting studies.

claim: A regenerated axolotl limb is a high fidelity replicate of the original limb comprised of the same cell lineages.
source: We find that a regenerated axolotl limb is a high fidelity replicate of the original limb comprised of the same cell lineages, with lineages that contribute to as little as one ten-thousandth of the original limb found in the regenerated limb at the same relative frequencies.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Lineages that contribute to as little as one ten-thousandth of the original limb are found in the regenerated limb at the same relative frequencies.
source: We find that a regenerated axolotl limb is a high fidelity replicate of the original limb comprised of the same cell lineages, with lineages that contribute to as little as one ten-thousandth of the original limb found in the regenerated limb at the same relative frequencies.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: This level of fidelity is maintained after multiple rounds of amputation and full limb regeneration.
source: This level of fidelity is maintained after multiple rounds of amputation and full limb regeneration.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data on repeated amputations.

claim: The salamander is now genetically tractable, in particular by using CRISPR/Cas-mediated mutagenesis.
source: These observations, and our quantification of this fidelity, may be of great importance to future studies as the salamander is now genetically tractable, in particular by using CRISPR/Cas-mediated mutagenesis (Flowers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Numerous studies using high-throughput gene expression analysis identified an expanding set of genes specifically upregulated in the axolotl limb blastema.
source: Numerous studies using high-throughput gene expression analysis identified an expanding set of genes specifically upregulated in the axolotl limb blastema (Bryant et al., 2017; Knapp et al., 2013; Voss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The abundance of uncharacterized targets of interest has created a demand for higher throughput methods to characterize the consequences of genetic manipulation on limb regeneration in mosaic F0 animals.
source: The abundance of uncharacterized targets of interest has created a demand for higher throughput methods to characterize the consequences of genetic manipulation on limb regeneration in mosaic F0 animals.
evidence: This is an inference about the state of the field based on the cited literature.

claim: This work establishes the baseline fidelity with which a regenerated axolotl limb is reconstructed with respect to embryonic lineages in mosaic animals.
source: This work establishes the baseline fidelity with which a regenerated axolotl limb is reconstructed with respect to embryonic lineages in such mosaic animals.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study.

claim: A similar approach may be used in the future to identify genes that when altered affect the ability of embryonic cell lineages to contribute to the regenerated limb.
source: In the future, a similar approach may be used to identify genes that when altered affect the ability of embryonic cell lineages to contribute to the regenerated limb.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the method.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas system was used to produce unique insertions and deletions at targeted genomic sites to independently genetically label numerous cell lineages in the developing axolotl embryo.
source: Here, we used the CRISPR/Cas system to produce unique insertions and deletions at targeted genomic sites to independently genetically label numerous cell lineages in the developing axolotl embryo.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Targeted mutations were induced during early embryonic development by microinjecting cas9 mRNA into the axolotl zygote with a single guideRNA (gRNA) against one of several genomic loci.
source: We induced targeted mutations during early embryonic development by microinjecting cas9 mRNA into the axolotl zygote with a single guideRNA (gRNA) against one of several genomic loci (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and references Figure 1a.

claim: The start and end points of induced insertions and deletions (indels) frequently vary with each event.
source: The start and end points of induced insertions and deletions (indels) frequently vary with each event, as do the precise identities of inserted sequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of CRISPR-induced mutations based on established knowledge.

claim: The precise identities of inserted sequences vary with each CRISPR-induced indel event.
source: The start and end points of induced insertions and deletions (indels) frequently vary with each event, as do the precise identities of inserted sequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of CRISPR-induced mutations based on established knowledge.

claim: Each indel labels the genome of the affected cell and its descendants.
source: Therefore, each indel labels the genome of the affected cell and its descendants (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an inference about how indels function as lineage labels, supported by Figure 1a.

claim: Two to four animals were targeted with one of six gRNAs to produce 19 animals with targeted mutations.
source: Using gRNAs effective at inducing high levels of mutagenesis that were not expected to have a deleterious impact on limb regeneration, we targeted two to four animals with one of six gRNAs to produce 19 animals with targeted mutations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: DNA was extracted from amputated original and fully regenerated limbs from the same individuals.
source: We extracted DNA from amputated original and fully regenerated limbs from the same individuals and performed Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) to identify all indels generated at the targeted sites for each gRNA.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) was performed to identify all indels generated at the targeted sites for each gRNA.
source: We extracted DNA from amputated original and fully regenerated limbs from the same individuals and performed Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) to identify all indels generated at the targeted sites for each gRNA.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: DNA extracted from the entire amputated limbs of mutagenized axolotls is mosaic and exhibits allelic heterogeneity.
source: NGS of PCR products of targeted genomic loci reveals that DNA extracted from the entire amputated limbs of mutagenized axolotls is mosaic and exhibits allelic heterogeneity (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; mean = 27.3 alleles, s.d. = ±10.2, n = 19 original limbs).
evidence: This is a finding from the NGS data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The mean number of alleles detected in original limbs is 27.3 with a standard deviation of ±10.2 (n = 19 original limbs).
source: NGS of PCR products of targeted genomic loci reveals that DNA extracted from the entire amputated limbs of mutagenized axolotls is mosaic and exhibits allelic heterogeneity (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; mean = 27.3 alleles, s.d. = ±10.2, n = 19 original limbs).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary limb predicts the log score of the normalized read number of each allele in the secondary limb (r2 = 0.37, p<1 × 10−15).
source: A simple linear regression indicates that the log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary limb predicts the log score of the normalized read number of each allele in the secondary limb (r2 = 0.37, p<1 × 10−15).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: Specific-allele-labelled cell populations contribute to both the original and regenerated limbs at similar frequencies.
source: Thus, specific-allele-labelled cell populations contribute to both the original and regenerated limbs at similar frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the linear regression analysis.

claim: The majority of the alleles detected in the limbs of animals in this study are low frequency (367/492 alleles represent less than 1.6% of all reads in the limb).
source: The majority of the alleles detected in the limbs of animals in this study are low frequency (i.e., represent less than 1.6% of all reads in the limb; 367/492 alleles, Figure 2a), with a median of 2332 reads per million (RPM).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 2a.

claim: Low frequency alleles have a median of 2332 reads per million (RPM).
source: The majority of the alleles detected in the limbs of animals in this study are low frequency (i.e., represent less than 1.6% of all reads in the limb; 367/492 alleles, Figure 2a), with a median of 2332 reads per million (RPM).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Low frequency alleles are more likely to increase in frequency or exhibit less than a one fold decrease (197/367 alleles) than to disappear (97/367 alleles).
source: When we examined the behavior of these alleles, we found that low frequency alleles are more likely to increase in frequency or exhibit less than a one fold decrease (197/367 alleles) than to disappear (97/367 alleles; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 2b.

claim: Low frequency cell lineages are highly preserved in the limb after regeneration.
source: Taken together, our work indicates that low frequency cell lineages are highly preserved in the limb after regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of low frequency allele behavior.

claim: In a representative case, the net difference in the RPM for all alleles before and after complete limb regeneration represents 10.1% of the total reads.
source: In this representative case, the net difference in the RPM for all alleles before and after complete limb regeneration represents 10.1% of the total reads (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from a specific case, supported by Figure 3b.

claim: Among the 19 animals in this study, the mean difference in allelic identities of original and secondary limbs was 24.2% (s.d. = ±16.1%).
source: We found that among the 19 animals in this study, the mean difference in allelic identities of original and secondary limbs was only 24.2% (s.d. = ±16.1%; Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis across all animals.

claim: The original limb of one animal (EGFP 4) exhibited spontaneous malformations and polydactyly at the time of the first amputation.
source: Interestingly, the original limb of one animal, EGFP 4, exhibited spontaneous malformations and polydactyly at the time of the first amputation (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed the highest change in allelic identity between limbs of all assessed animals, 63.3%.
evidence: This is an observation from the study, supported by figures.

claim: Animal EGFP 4 showed the highest change in allelic identity between limbs of all assessed animals, 63.3%.
source: Interestingly, the original limb of one animal, EGFP 4, exhibited spontaneous malformations and polydactyly at the time of the first amputation (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed the highest change in allelic identity between limbs of all assessed animals, 63.3%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The change in allelic identity reflects the morphological fidelity of regeneration.
source: This suggests that the change in allelic identity reflects the morphological fidelity of regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of the malformed limb showing the highest change in allelic identity.

claim: Removing the EGFP 4 case reduces the mean difference in allelic identity between original and secondary limbs to 22.0% (s.d. = ±13.6%).
source: Removing this case reduces the mean difference in allelic identity between original and secondary limbs to 22.0% (s.d. = ±13.6%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis after excluding an outlier.

claim: There is no significant correlation between overall mutation rate or number of alleles and the change in allelic identity of regenerated limbs (R2 = 0.14, p=0.11 for mutation rate and identity; R2 = 0.01, p=0.76 for mutation rate and total number of alleles).
source: There is no significant correlation between overall mutation rate or number of alleles and the change in allelic identity of regenerated limbs (R2 = 0.14, p=0.11 for mutation rate and identity; R2 = 0.01, p=0.76 for mutation rate and total number of alleles).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: A newly regenerated limb is a surprisingly high fidelity replica of the original limb.
source: These findings demonstrate that a newly regenerated limb is a surprisingly high fidelity replica of the original limb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative findings on allelic identity changes.

claim: Salamanders such as axolotls and newts can regenerate the same structures repeatedly throughout life.
source: Salamanders such as axolotls and newts can regenerate the same structures repeatedly throughout life, though the rate and fidelity of such regeneration can decline with age or after metamorphosis (Monaghan et al., 2014; Seifert and Voss, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The rate and fidelity of regeneration can decline with age or after metamorphosis in salamanders.
source: Salamanders such as axolotls and newts can regenerate the same structures repeatedly throughout life, though the rate and fidelity of such regeneration can decline with age or after metamorphosis (Monaghan et al., 2014; Seifert and Voss, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: After full regeneration of secondary limbs, a second amputation was carried out on the limbs of 12 embryonically mutagenized animals.
source: After full regeneration of secondary limbs, we carried out a second amputation of the limbs of 12 embryonically mutagenized animals, permitted full tertiary limb growth, subsequently amputated those limbs, and used NGS to identify and quantify each allele at the targeted sites (Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for repeated amputations.

claim: The log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary predicts the log score of the normalized read number of each allele in the tertiary limb (r2 = 0.47, p<1 × 10−15).
source: A simple linear regression reveals that the log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary predicts the log score of the normalized read number of each allele in the tertiary limb (r2 = 0.47, p<1 × 10−15; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 4b.

claim: The allelic identities of tertiary limbs differed very little from those of the secondary limbs (mean = 15.8%, s.d. = ±6.5%).
source: Furthermore, we found that the allelic identities of these tertiary limbs differed very little from those of the secondary limbs (mean = 15.8%, s.d. = ±6.5%; Figure 4c; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: There is not a decline in morphological fidelity after repeated amputations.
source: Thus, just as there is not a decline in morphological fidelity after repeated amputations, there is no decline in the fidelity of cell lineages that comprise the limb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of allelic identities across multiple regenerations.

claim: There is no decline in the fidelity of cell lineages that comprise the limb after repeated amputations.
source: Thus, just as there is not a decline in morphological fidelity after repeated amputations, there is no decline in the fidelity of cell lineages that comprise the limb.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on tertiary limb regeneration.

claim: Previous studies have indicated that CRISPR-induced indels are not truly random, as particular indels arise more frequently than others after mutagenesis with a single gRNA.
source: Previous studies have indicated that CRISPR-induced indels are not truly random, as particular indels arise more frequently than others after mutagenesis with a single gRNA (Gagnon et al., 2014; Burger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The majority of allele sequences appeared in only one animal out of as many as four animals mutagenized with a single gRNA.
source: However, comparing the identity of alleles across individuals shows that the majority of allele sequences appeared in only one animal out of the as many as four animals mutagenized with a single gRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: For gRNAs assessed in four animals, individual alleles that received fewer than 1.6% of all sequence reads in an individual appeared in only one or two animals.
source: For gRNAs assessed in four animals, the individual alleles that received fewer than 1.6% of all sequence reads in an individual (which we will refer to as low frequency alleles) appeared in only one or two animals, while all alleles that received more reads per individual were found in multiple animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: All alleles that received more than 1.6% of reads per individual were found in multiple animals.
source: For gRNAs assessed in four animals, the individual alleles that received fewer than 1.6% of all sequence reads in an individual (which we will refer to as low frequency alleles) appeared in only one or two animals, while all alleles that received more reads per individual were found in multiple animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: At concentrations of cas9 that produced no or single-digit numbers of alleles at each target in each embryo (mean = 1.4 alleles, s.d. =±1.6, n = 50, 5 targets tested in 10 animals each), the majority of alleles were unique (26/39 alleles).
source: At concentrations of cas9 that produced no or single-digit numbers of alleles at each target in each embryo (mean = 1.4 alleles, s.d. =±1.6, n = 50, 5 targets tested in 10 animals each), the majority of alleles were unique (26/39 alleles; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experiment with reduced cas9 concentrations, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Though some alleles are favorably produced from targeted mutagenesis, most alleles are formed with sufficiently low probabilities as to represent unique cell lineages even in highly mosaic mutant animals.
source: Together, these results suggest that, though some alleles are favorably produced from targeted mutagenesis, most alleles are formed with sufficiently low probabilities as to represent unique cell lineages even in highly mosaic mutant animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the allelic diversity data.

claim: Subsequent amputations were carried out from regenerated forelimbs of four mutagenized animals for tissue analysis.
source: To address whether unique cell lineages are tissue-restricted, we carried out subsequent amputations from regenerated forelimbs of four mutagenized animals.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Blood samples, hand, and dissected nerve, blood vessel, bone/cartilage, skin, and muscle were collected from each of four animals for DNA extraction and NGS.
source: After these amputations, from each animal we extracted blood samples, collected the hand from the amputated forelimb, and dissected nerve, blood vessel, bone/cartilage, skin, and muscle from the remaining amputated forelimb. We then extracted DNA from the hand and the tissue-enriched samples and carried out NGS of PCR products of the targeted genomic loci in each tissue.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for tissue-specific analysis.

claim: High frequency alleles (those representing greater than 6.5% of all reads) of the whole hand could be detected in all or almost all of the six individual tissue-enriched DNA samples from the same limb (mean = 5.4 of 6 tissues, s.d. = ±1.1, n = 15/171 alleles).
source: NGS revealed that the high frequency alleles (i.e., those representing greater than 6.5% of all reads) of the whole hand could be detected in all or almost all of the six individual tissue-enriched DNA samples from the same limb (mean = 5.4 of 6 tissues, s.d. = ±1.1, n = 15/171 alleles, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific NGS analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Alleles that appear at a low frequency within the hand (those that represent less than 1.6% of all reads) are found in fewer tissues (mean = 2.8 of 6 tissues, s.d. =±1.6, n = 135 alleles).
source: Conversely, alleles that appear at a low frequency within the hand (i.e., those that represent less than 1.6% of all reads) are found in fewer tissues (mean = 2.8 of 6 tissues, s.d. =±1.6, n = 135 alleles, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific NGS analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Each tissue-enriched sample contains alleles exhibiting more than a 16-fold enrichment in normalized reads relative to all other tissues (29/171 alleles).
source: We find that each tissue-enriched sample contains alleles exhibiting more than a 16-fold enrichment in normalized reads relative to all other tissues (29/171 alleles), and 29 additional alleles were found to be similarly enriched in only two tissues.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific NGS analysis.

claim: 29 additional alleles were found to be enriched in only two tissues.
source: We find that each tissue-enriched sample contains alleles exhibiting more than a 16-fold enrichment in normalized reads relative to all other tissues (29/171 alleles), and 29 additional alleles were found to be similarly enriched in only two tissues.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific NGS analysis.

claim: Blood was the source of the most tissue-enriched alleles (17/58 alleles).
source: From all tissue samples, we found that the blood was the source of the most tissue-enriched alleles (17/58 alleles) likely arising from the distant origins of hematopoietic cells and the ease with which blood may be isolated (Lopez et al., 2014; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific NGS analysis, with citation supporting the interpretation.

claim: Blood-enriched alleles likely arise from the distant origins of hematopoietic cells and the ease with which blood may be isolated.
source: From all tissue samples, we found that the blood was the source of the most tissue-enriched alleles (17/58 alleles) likely arising from the distant origins of hematopoietic cells and the ease with which blood may be isolated (Lopez et al., 2014; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Skin-enriched alleles were disproportionally represented both among alleles that decreased in frequency from primary to secondary limbs and among those that increased in frequency from secondary to tertiary limbs (two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.02; p=0.05, respectively).
source: We found that the only source of tissue-enriched alleles that underwent any significant change was skin, as skin-enriched alleles were disproportionally represented both among alleles that decreased in frequency from primary to secondary limbs and among those that increased in frequency from secondary to tertiary limbs (skin-enriched alleles = 14/58 tissue-enriched alleles, 8/14 tissue-enriched alleles decreasing from primary to secondary, 9/17 alleles increasing from secondary to tertiary; two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.02; p=0.05, respectively; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Skin-enriched alleles were dramatically overrepresented in skin compared to cartilage/bone (14,103-fold greater RPM, s.d.= ±15,680 RPM, n = 14 alleles).
source: We found that skin-enriched alleles were dramatically overrepresented in skin compared to cartilage/bone (14,103-fold greater RPM, s.d.= ±15,680 RPM, n = 14 alleles); thus, these changes in the levels of skin-enriched alleles in the limb likely reflect the migration of epidermal cells from outside of the wound site to contribute to the regenerating skin rather than dermal cells that contribute to cartilage (Currie et al., 2016; Seifert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Changes in the levels of skin-enriched alleles in the limb likely reflect the migration of epidermal cells from outside of the wound site to contribute to the regenerating skin rather than dermal cells that contribute to cartilage.
source: We found that skin-enriched alleles were dramatically overrepresented in skin compared to cartilage/bone (14,103-fold greater RPM, s.d.= ±15,680 RPM, n = 14 alleles); thus, these changes in the levels of skin-enriched alleles in the limb likely reflect the migration of epidermal cells from outside of the wound site to contribute to the regenerating skin rather than dermal cells that contribute to cartilage (Currie et al., 2016; Seifert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within the whole hand, tissue-enriched alleles are almost exclusively found among low frequency alleles (57/58 alleles).
source: Within the whole hand, such tissue-enriched alleles are almost exclusively found among low frequency alleles (57/58 alleles), and together they represent a minor proportion of the total sequence reads within the hand (mean = 7.8%, s.d. = ±8.6%, n = 4 hands, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Tissue-enriched alleles together represent a minor proportion of the total sequence reads within the hand (mean = 7.8%, s.d. = ±8.6%, n = 4 hands).
source: Within the whole hand, such tissue-enriched alleles are almost exclusively found among low frequency alleles (57/58 alleles), and together they represent a minor proportion of the total sequence reads within the hand (mean = 7.8%, s.d. = ±8.6%, n = 4 hands, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Of 58 alleles found to be tissue-enriched, 27 were not detected in sequence reads from the whole hand.
source: Of 58 alleles found to be tissue-enriched, 27 were not detected in sequence reads from the whole hand, and such alleles were exclusively low frequency within the tissues in which they were enriched.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Tissue-enriched alleles not detected in the whole hand were exclusively low frequency within the tissues in which they were enriched.
source: Of 58 alleles found to be tissue-enriched, 27 were not detected in sequence reads from the whole hand, and such alleles were exclusively low frequency within the tissues in which they were enriched.
evidence: This is a finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: All tissue-enriched alleles that could not be detected within the hand represent 0.43% (s.d. = ±0.63%, n = 24 tissue-enriched samples) of all reads within the tissues in which they are enriched.
source: Together, all such tissue-enriched alleles that could not be detected within the hand represent 0.43% (s.d. = ±0.63%, n = 24 tissue-enriched samples) of all reads within the tissues in which they are enriched, and thus, were likely under-sampled rather than absent in the hand.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Tissue-enriched alleles that could not be detected within the hand were likely under-sampled rather than absent in the hand.
source: Together, all such tissue-enriched alleles that could not be detected within the hand represent 0.43% (s.d. = ±0.63%, n = 24 tissue-enriched samples) of all reads within the tissues in which they are enriched, and thus, were likely under-sampled rather than absent in the hand.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low frequency of these alleles.

claim: High-frequency alleles account for most of the sequence reads obtained in single limbs and are broadly distributed throughout tissues.
source: These comparisons among alleles from different tissue samples indicate that high-frequency alleles account for most of the sequence reads obtained in single limbs and are broadly distributed throughout tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: High-frequency alleles either form in the early blastula stages of embryogenesis, or independently in multiple cell lineages, or both.
source: Such alleles either form in the early blastula stages of embryogenesis, or independently in multiple cell lineages, or both.
evidence: This is an inference about the origin of high-frequency alleles.

claim: Low-frequency alleles that form at later developmental stages are more likely to exhibit tissue-specific enrichment.
source: While low-frequency alleles that form at later developmental stages are more likely to exhibit tissue-specific enrichment, such tissue-enriched alleles often occur at such low frequencies as to not be detectable within entire limb samples using NGS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: Tissue-enriched alleles often occur at such low frequencies as to not be detectable within entire limb samples using NGS.
source: While low-frequency alleles that form at later developmental stages are more likely to exhibit tissue-specific enrichment, such tissue-enriched alleles often occur at such low frequencies as to not be detectable within entire limb samples using NGS.
evidence: This is a finding from the tissue-specific analysis.

claim: The allele identities and frequencies found in nerve, blood vessel, and blood-enriched samples exhibit very low correlations with each other and with those from other tissue-enriched samples.
source: We find that the allele identities and frequencies found in nerve, blood vessel, and blood-enriched samples exhibit very low correlations with each other and with those from other tissue-enriched samples (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, supported by Figure 5a.

claim: Alleles in the muscle and skin exhibit both higher correlations with each other and with those found within the entire hand than to those of other tissue-enriched samples.
source: Alleles in the muscle and skin exhibit both higher correlations with each other and with those found within the entire hand than to those of other tissue-enriched samples (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, supported by Figure 5a.

claim: The similarities in allelic composition between muscle, skin, and hand are likely partially due to the overrepresentation of these tissues within the hand.
source: These similarities are likely partially due to the overrepresentation of these tissues within the hand, as well as the fact that such dissected samples from the muscle and skin of the limb contain significant contributions from multiple tissues.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed correlations.

claim: Dissected samples from the muscle and skin of the limb contain significant contributions from multiple tissues.
source: These similarities are likely partially due to the overrepresentation of these tissues within the hand, as well as the fact that such dissected samples from the muscle and skin of the limb contain significant contributions from multiple tissues.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the tissue samples.

claim: The variation in the allelic compositions of the regenerated tissue-enriched samples indicate that they are differently reconstituted with respect to their embryonic origins.
source: Nonetheless, as these tissue-enriched samples were derived from fully regenerated limbs, the variation in the allelic compositions of the regenerated tissue-enriched samples indicate that they are differently reconstituted with respect to their embryonic origins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variation in allelic compositions across tissues.

claim: Some alleles present in original limbs were not detected in secondary limbs.
source: Our sequencing results indicate that limb regeneration is a high fidelity process as the embryonic lineages that are detected in the original limb are retained after multiple rounds of regeneration at similar frequencies; however, we do find that some alleles present in original limbs were not detected in secondary limbs.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The apparent bimodality of the distribution in changes in allele frequencies between primary and secondary limbs is reflected in Figure 2b.
source: This is reflected in the apparent bimodality of the distribution in changes in allele frequencies between primary and secondary limbs depicted in Figure 2b.
evidence: This is an observation about the data distribution, supported by Figure 2b.

claim: Of 54 alleles lost between primary and secondary limbs in 4 animals examined for three rounds of regeneration, 35 were found to be present in subsequent limbs or tissues.
source: In the limbs of 4 animals that were examined for three rounds of regeneration, of 54 alleles lost between primary and secondary limbs, 35 were found to be present in subsequent limbs or tissues.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of alleles across multiple regenerations.

claim: 5/5 alleles detected in the secondary limbs but not in the original limbs were found in subsequent regenerated limbs or tissues from the same animal.
source: While novel alleles appeared in subsequent limbs, 5/5 such alleles detected in the secondary limbs but not in the original limbs were found in subsequent regenerated limbs or tissues from the same animal (4/6 alleles detected in the tertiary, but not primary limb, were detected in other iterations of the limb; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of alleles across multiple regenerations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 4/6 alleles detected in the tertiary, but not primary limb, were detected in other iterations of the limb.
source: While novel alleles appeared in subsequent limbs, 5/5 such alleles detected in the secondary limbs but not in the original limbs were found in subsequent regenerated limbs or tissues from the same animal (4/6 alleles detected in the tertiary, but not primary limb, were detected in other iterations of the limb; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of alleles across multiple regenerations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The disproportionate number of unrecovered alleles from the primary to secondary limb compared to those from the secondary or tertiary to primary limbs indicates that some cell lineages are truly lost upon limb regeneration while others were not detected due to under-sampling.
source: The disproportionate number of unrecovered alleles from the primary to secondary limb compared to those from the secondary or tertiary to primary limbs indicates that some cell lineages are truly lost upon limb regeneration while others were not detected, most likely due to under-sampling at the initial DNA amplification step.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of allele recovery across regenerations.

claim: The average allele present in the original limb that is subsequently undetectable after regeneration is a rare component of the limb (mean = 748 RPM, s.d. =±1656, median = 20 RPM, n = 19/154 alleles detected in the original limb).
source: The average allele present in the original limb that is subsequently undetectable after regeneration is a rare component of the limb (mean = 748 RPM, s.d. =±1656, median = 20 RPM, n = 19/154 alleles detected in the original limb).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of lost alleles.

claim: The sum of lost cell lineages in each limb investigated represents a minor portion of the cell lineages comprising the limb (0.34%, ±0.56%, n = 4 limbs).
source: The sum of such lost cell lineages in each limb investigated represents a minor portion of the cell lineages comprising the limb (0.34%, ±0.56%, n = 4 limbs), indicating that either a subset of embryonically-labeled cell lineages are unable to participate in limb regeneration or that some cell lineages become isolated in distal regions of the limb that are consequently lost after amputation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of lost alleles.

claim: Either a subset of embryonically-labeled cell lineages are unable to participate in limb regeneration or some cell lineages become isolated in distal regions of the limb that are consequently lost after amputation.
source: The sum of such lost cell lineages in each limb investigated represents a minor portion of the cell lineages comprising the limb (0.34%, ±0.56%, n = 4 limbs), indicating that either a subset of embryonically-labeled cell lineages are unable to participate in limb regeneration or that some cell lineages become isolated in distal regions of the limb that are consequently lost after amputation.
evidence: This is an inference about the possible explanations for lost alleles.

claim: Studies using transgenic tissue grafts in the axolotl have provided a powerful means to track the behaviors of cells and tissues of differing origins during limb regeneration.
source: In recent years, studies using transgenic tissue grafts in the axolotl have provided a powerful means to track the behaviors of cells and tissues of differing origins during limb regeneration (Kragl et al., 2009; Maden et al., 2015; McCusker et al., 2016; Nacu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A growing consensus exists that the role of transdifferentiation of tissues in limb regeneration is minimal in salamanders, with cells of regenerating tissues largely arising from cells of the same embryonic origin.
source: Such studies have created a growing consensus that the role of transdifferentiation of tissues in limb regeneration is minimal in salamanders, with cells of regenerating tissues largely arising from cells of the same embryonic origin (Kragl et al., 2009); yet, the scope of such grafting work has been limited as only the fates of tissues derived from single large tissue grafts could be assessed in one limb at a time.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The scope of grafting work has been limited as only the fates of tissues derived from single large tissue grafts could be assessed in one limb at a time.
source: Such studies have created a growing consensus that the role of transdifferentiation of tissues in limb regeneration is minimal in salamanders, with cells of regenerating tissues largely arising from cells of the same embryonic origin (Kragl et al., 2009); yet, the scope of such grafting work has been limited as only the fates of tissues derived from single large tissue grafts could be assessed in one limb at a time.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Recent efforts have coupled tissue grafting with tissue-specific transgenic lines and in vivo imaging of cell behaviors during appendage regeneration to elucidate this process with spatial and temporal resolution.
source: More recent efforts have coupled this approach with tissue-specific transgenic lines and in vivo imaging of cell behaviors during appendage regeneration to elucidate this process with spatial and temporal resolution (Currie et al., 2016; Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent studies continue to demonstrate that regenerated tissues arise from tissues of a similar origin.
source: Such works continue to demonstrate that regenerated tissues arise from tissues of a similar origin, though some ambiguity remains.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from recent research.

claim: Two recent studies demonstrate that cartilage and bone make little, if any, contribution to skeletal regeneration.
source: For instance, two recent studies demonstrate that cartilage and bone make little, if any, contribution to skeletal regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016), with dermal fibroblasts appearing to give rise to most regenerative connective tissues during digit tip regeneration (Currie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dermal fibroblasts appear to give rise to most regenerative connective tissues during digit tip regeneration.
source: For instance, two recent studies demonstrate that cartilage and bone make little, if any, contribution to skeletal regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016), with dermal fibroblasts appearing to give rise to most regenerative connective tissues during digit tip regeneration (Currie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The genetic labeling approach applied in this study can quantify the relative contributions of numerous, often very low frequency cell lineages to limb regeneration at once.
source: With the genetic labeling approach applied in our study, we can quantify the relative contributions of numerous, often very low frequency cell lineages to limb regeneration at once.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the method used in the study.

claim: Low frequency populations of cells do not largely repopulate the regenerated limb at the expense of others.
source: We can infer from our data that low frequency populations of cells do not largely repopulate the regenerated limb at the expense of others.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on allele frequency preservation.

claim: The same embryonic lineages that produce the limb faithfully regenerate the limb in the same proportions.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that the same embryonic lineages that produce the limb faithfully regenerate the limb in the same proportions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The conclusions of this study do not challenge the recent observations that bone and cartilage give rise to little or no skeletal tissues after regeneration.
source: These conclusions do not challenge the recent observations that bone and cartilage give rise to little or no skeletal tissues after regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016), but indicate that the cells that replace amputated bone and cartilage are most likely derived from the same embryonic cell lineages that initially formed the lost bone and cartilage.
evidence: This is a statement about how the current findings relate to previous research.

claim: The cells that replace amputated bone and cartilage are most likely derived from the same embryonic cell lineages that initially formed the lost bone and cartilage.
source: These conclusions do not challenge the recent observations that bone and cartilage give rise to little or no skeletal tissues after regeneration (Currie et al., 2016; McCusker et al., 2016), but indicate that the cells that replace amputated bone and cartilage are most likely derived from the same embryonic cell lineages that initially formed the lost bone and cartilage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Zygotic injection of cas9 and individual gRNAs achieves a high rate of mutagenesis.
source: Zygotic injection of cas9 and individual gRNAs achieves a high rate of mutagenesis, but the majority of cells are labeled with mutations that occur in either the earliest cell divisions or multiple times throughout development.
evidence: This is a finding about the method used in the study.

claim: The majority of cells are labeled with mutations that occur in either the earliest cell divisions or multiple times throughout development when using zygotic injection of cas9 and individual gRNAs.

claim: Labeling redundancy could be reduced by the application of multiple gRNAs within a single amplifiable region.
source: Such labeling redundancy could be reduced by the application of multiple gRNAs within a single amplifiable region.

claim: The comparatively long generation time of the axolotl makes the generation of stable, single-copy transgenic lines a time consuming task.
source: Alternately, while the comparatively long generation time of the axolotl makes the generation of stable, single-copy transgenic lines a time consuming task, synthetic transgenic arrays of CRISPR targets (McKenna et al., 2016) may be eventually employed to create higher density allelic maps.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of working with axolotls.

source: This study marks the first example by which regeneration has been characterized using a CRISPR-derived lineage tracing approach, and we find that the regenerated limb is repopulated by embryonic cell lineages in a manner that recapitulates the development of the original limb.
